name: ctx-oriental
_comment: Persian / Middle-Eastern Yamaha styles -> Casio CT-X, using the
ORIENTAL hand-drum kit on the percussion part.
Pair it with an oriental template and the richest standard kit on the
drum part -- the factory Arabic rhythms are built this way:
./y2c.py convert STYLE -o OUT.AC7 --map maps/ctx-oriental.json \
--template 'Baladi X3000.AC7' --clear-unused --tone drum=0/120
WHY TWO TABLES. The two Casio drum parts hold different kits. Kit 52
is hand drums only: notes 59 and 69-80, nothing else. GM note numbers
sent there are silent, so the percussion part needs its own targets.
The drum part keeps a standard kit and so keeps the shared table.
WHERE THE NUMBERS COME FROM. Casio publishes no drum assignment list,
so none of this was looked up. Targets on the percussion part are
restricted to notes the factory Arabic rhythms demonstrably strike in
kit 52. Note 69 is the doum and 71 the tak, established by position in
three rhythms whose patterns differ: Malfouf is doum-tak-tak, Baladi
is doum-doum-tak-doum-tak, 69 lands on the doums of both, and
Khaliji's kick doubles 69 exactly. 73 is the lighter tak, 70 the riq.
Notes 35-87 are mapped by their GM meaning, reliable because Yamaha
styles follow GM there. Notes 12-34 and 88-93 are Yamaha oriental
articulations with no GM meaning; those are INFERRED from measured
velocity and beat alignment across all 46 styles, and are the ones to
check by ear first. `y2c report STYLE --map ...` prints both parts.
